_: Where the numbers are on the screen.
EVERY BOX IN THIS FILE IS AN ESTIMATE UNTIL calibrate.py HAS RUN.
They were written from the standard 1080p Apex layout without a real frame
to check against, which makes them a good starting point and nothing more.
The pipeline around them is finished; these four numbers per field are not.
Run `python calibrate.py` with the game open, look at the boxes it draws on
a real screenshot, and drag them until they sit on the digits. Then set
`calibrated` to true so the watcher stops warning about it on startup.
Boxes are [x0, y0, x1, y1] as fractions of the CENTRED 16:9 SAFE AREA, not
of the monitor. Apex anchors its menus to 16:9 and fills the sides, so on an
ultrawide a fraction of the screen lands somewhere else entirely. See
ocr.safe_area(). This is also why these boxes work unchanged at 1440p.
The screen that matters: it carries the match's real numbers.
Reached after the squad is out, and it sits there for long enough that
the reader gets its several looks. The player's own row is the first
one; squadmates' rows are deliberately not read — their stats are not
Ric's to publish.
A win. Same summary follows it, so this screen exists only to set
place=1 with certainty rather than trusting an OCR read of '#1' —
a 1 is the digit most often invented out of a UI edge, and a fake
win is the single most embarrassing thing this could publish.
The account-wide panel — lobby, gamertag, career. The only place
these totals exist anywhere: no API on any platform returns them,
which is why they have been typed in by hand until now.
Read whenever Ric happens to open it. Never on a timer, because
opening it for the watcher would mean the watcher was making him do
something, which is the exact thing this is supposed to end.
A legend's three equipped trackers, on the banner in the lobby or on
the legend select screen. This is the same keyhole the ALS API reads
through — but read here it costs no API call, needs no key, and
updates the moment he scrolls past the legend instead of tomorrow.
The cheap test that runs on every frame so the expensive one does not.
OCR on a 1080p frame costs tens of milliseconds; at four frames a second
that is real CPU taken from a game running on the same machine, forever,
to answer 'no' about a frame of someone walking around Storm Point.
So first: shrink the frame to a thumbnail and look at how bright it is.
Apex's summary and menu screens are dark, flat scrims. Live gameplay is
neither. Anything that fails this never reaches Tesseract, and the
watcher costs about a millisecond a frame while he is actually playing.
